nodes.label: Add name or position change dialog
nodes.norm_label: add name or position change dialog
nodes.rationale: Door 2: closes the open version and starts a new one, the "record a change that happened" path, opened from the employees table row menu.

nodes.label: Correct this entry dialog
nodes.rationale: Door 3: edits one existing version in place from the history sheet, carrying the warning headed "This corrects what is already filed".

nodes.label: Name and position history sheet
nodes.rationale: A shadcn-svelte sheet rather than a dialog, because the content is a list of unknown length and is read far more often than written. Named from four plain candidates: "Name history" promised less than the screen shows, "Change history" does not say change of what, "Employee history" sounds like hire and leave dates, and Service Record is a real CSC document carrying salary and appointment data this system does not store. Entries are fetched when the panel opens rather than with the page.

nodes.label: Correcting an entry versus recording a change
nodes.norm_label: correcting an entry versus recording a change
nodes.rationale: A typing mistake was never correct so filed documents should be repaired; a marriage or promotion was correct at the time so old documents must keep the old value. The user replaced a question-at-save-time design with two separate entry points, so the button pressed already says which case it is and nothing has to be inferred or asked halfway through a save. A correction touches only the version being looked at; a closed version is corrected deliberately from the history panel.

nodes.label: Remedial preference hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Fixes are proposed in order: delete the animation, reduce it, fix the easing, fix the origin and physicality, make it interruptible, move it to the GPU, make the timing asymmetric, polish, then accessibility and cohesion. Deleting comes first because when motion's rightness is uncertain the strongest move is often removal.

nodes.label: Fuel is the only area with an approval step
nodes.norm_label: fuel is the only area with an approval step
nodes.rationale: A staff member requests a withdrawal slip and GSU approves it, but the approval itself is physical — somebody signs the printed slip and afterwards it is marked approved in the system. So the system records an approval that already happened on paper; it is not where the approving takes place. Approvers may approve their own submissions, which matches actual agency practice and is deliberate, not an oversight.

nodes.label: One role per user, no per-user overrides
nodes.norm_label: one role per user, no per-user overrides
nodes.rationale: Roles today are Admin, GSU and per-section Encoder/Focal roles, with the exact section-to-role mapping still to be decided. The small scale is why several design decisions accept a small residual risk rather than build machinery against it.

nodes.label: DENR Agency Logo (Department of Environment and Natural Resources)
nodes.norm_label: denr agency logo (department of environment and natural resources)

nodes.label: backfill-employee-history script (2000-01-01 start)
nodes.rationale: Safe to run twice because it skips anybody who already has a version. Backfilled versions start at 2000-01-01 rather than the run date because paper is always typed in after it was signed, so a slip filed last week must still find its signatories; Topic 8 of the signatory document already ruled out reports for periods before go-live.

nodes.label: endSessionsForEmployee helper
nodes.rationale: Shared by the `separate` action and by `update` when the edit is what marks somebody as having left; the editor was the second way in and would otherwise have left the person signed in.

nodes.label: Duplicate employee check
nodes.rationale: Exact match on first name, last name and birth date refuses the save; a birth-date match with a different name, or a name match where one record has no birth date, only warns and lets the admin decide. Written once in duplicate-check.ts and run both live in the dialog and in the server actions, which cannot be bypassed. Edits run the same check, excluding the record being edited.

nodes.label: employee_history table (versions)
nodes.rationale: One row per version of a person's name, position title and short form, with valid_from and valid_until. Documents point at a version rather than at the person, so a marriage or a promotion cannot rewrite paperwork already filed. employee keeps its own copy as the current value so an ordinary lookup stays one read, and both tables are written in one transaction by one function.

nodes.label: employee table
nodes.rationale: One row per person in the office whether or not they log in. Holds name, position_title, position_short_form, org_unit_fk, birth_date, sex, civil_status, tenure_status, employment_status. No employee number, because COS and Job Order staff hold no plantilla item so the column would be empty for much of the office.

nodes.label: Lockout through the Employees page
nodes.rationale: Sign-in asks two questions (is the account active, does this person still work here) while every other part of the system asks only the first, so the state "account active, employee separated" locks somebody out while the rest of the system thinks the account is fine. The Employees page gains the guards the Users page already has: no separating yourself, and no leaving zero super admins who can actually sign in. The password reset script also reports success on an account that cannot be used.

nodes.label: position_short_form
nodes.rationale: The boxes on the paper forms are small, so documents print "AO-I/Supply Officer" rather than "Administrative Officer I (Supply Officer)"; no rule worth trusting derives one from the other, so somebody types it once. Nullable, because a non-null column would have made the backfill impossible without inventing values. The rule that it must be present belongs to the document that prints it, which must refuse to print rather than leave a blank line.
nodes.source_location: Topic 9 — Why the short form is allowed to be empty

nodes.label: Bring this person back (reinstate)
nodes.rationale: An exact match on somebody who has left offers reinstatement inside the form rather than a bare refusal, because otherwise an admin changes a spelling to force the save and creates the duplicate the check exists to prevent. It also applies the typed position, section, tenure and civil status, since people rarely return to the same job, and the alert lists each change as old to new.

nodes.label: tenure_status (seven CSC categories)
nodes.rationale: permanent, temporary, casual, coterminous, contractual, cos, job_order. COS and JO sit apart because those people are engaged under a separate joint circular rather than CSC rules. `substitute` was excluded because the office never fills a post while its holder is on long leave. Displayed as "Type of appointment" rather than "Tenure".

nodes.label: user table (login only)
nodes.rationale: Holds only sign-in facts: username, password_hash, role_fk, account_status, must_change_password, failed_login_attempts, locked_until, last_login_at. Name fields moved to employee because a person has one name whether or not they sign in.

nodes.label: Birth date as the identity anchor
nodes.norm_label: birth date as the identity anchor
nodes.rationale: A birth date never changes: not on marriage, not on rehire, and it is the same for any tenure. An earlier system branched on the sex field to allow for a changed surname, but sex can be mistyped and then the whole check silently behaves differently, so that branch was dropped. The form and the server require a birth date while the column stays nullable, which keeps the "one record has no birth date" rule from being dead code.
nodes.source_location: Topic 7a — the birth date is the anchor, not the name

nodes.label: create-admin.ts asks instead of inventing a person
nodes.norm_label: create-admin.ts asks instead of inventing a person
nodes.rationale: The script used to write a placeholder "Admin User" employee with position System Administrator and tenure Permanent, which contradicted the whole argument for requiring the employee link and left a fake row in the Employees list. It already interviews whoever runs it for a username, so the real name, position, appointment type and birth date join the same run, and it opens the first history entry with its own SQL.

nodes.label: drizzle-kit push is unsafe on this project
nodes.norm_label: drizzle-kit push is unsafe on this project
nodes.rationale: Asked to add employee_history it also offered to repair earlier drift, and its way of adding a NOT NULL rule to a MySQL column is to TRUNCATE the table first; with --force it attempted that on employee and was saved only by the foreign key from user. Schema changes are applied as plain SQL instead.
nodes.source_location: Topic 9 — Applying it to the database

nodes.label: Employee and user full separation
nodes.rationale: Option 1 (full separation) was chosen over leaving user untouched or letting user double as the employee table, because the office's people would otherwise live in two tables, and because making login code responsible for always excluding password-less rows is easy to get wrong later.
nodes.source_location: Topic 10 origin / Where this comes from

nodes.label: employment_status kept at active/separated
nodes.rationale: Recording why somebody left (retirement, resignation, dismissal) overlaps with a personnel system; EMS is an environmental management system, so that belongs in an HR system if the agency ever gets one.

nodes.label: employee_history cascades where everything else restricts
nodes.norm_label: employee_history cascades where everything else restricts
nodes.rationale: With restrict every employee would become undeletable the moment the backfill gave them a first version, breaking the delete button even for somebody added by mistake. The protection arrives from the other side instead: a document holds a history row with restrict, so deleting that employee fails at the cascade and the person stays.

nodes.label: Mark as employed (undoing a mistaken separation)
nodes.norm_label: mark as employed (undoing a mistaken separation)
nodes.rationale: Separating closes the open version and reinstating opens a new one, so the pair is not an undo: the history shows a break in service that never happened and documents dated inside the gap find nobody. The missing operation reopens the closed version instead. One neutral menu item, mirroring "Mark as no longer employed", then a dialog asks whether the person really left or the record was a mistake — a question anybody can answer without being taught, unlike the correct-versus-change split in Topic 10. "Mark as employed again" was rejected because "again" answers the question the dialog is about to ask.

nodes.label: One employee, one login (unique employee_fk)
nodes.rationale: user.employee_fk is required and unique. Required because the sidebar name lives on the employee row, so a login with no employee is a login with no name and every screen would need an extra branch. Unique because the system records who did what, and two accounts for one human make "who changed this?" unanswerable.

nodes.label: role_fk stays on the login
nodes.rationale: "Role in the office" is position_title on employee; "role in the app" is a permission bundle. On employee, role_fk would be empty for most of the office and every reader would first have to check whether the person even has a login — a check easy to forget.

nodes.label: Sign-in refuses anyone no longer employed
nodes.norm_label: sign-in refuses anyone no longer employed
nodes.rationale: Option C beat switching the account off at the same moment (option B) because B leaves a gap: an admin could switch the account back on without touching the employment record. validateSessionToken deletes a session whose employee is not active, the login joins employee and refuses before looking at account status, and the Users page shows a "Person has left" badge so a dead account never reads plain Active.

nodes.label: Four distinct status columns
nodes.rationale: employment_status, civil_status and tenure_status on employee plus account_status (renamed from status) on user. The same word must never be reused across the two tables or whoever writes a query later reads the wrong one; "separated" unavoidably appears in two of them with different meanings.

nodes.label: Super admin handover is a new account, not a shared password
nodes.norm_label: super admin handover is a new account, not a shared password
nodes.rationale: Passing one admin login down between post-holders destroys attribution. Instead a second super admin user is created and the old one deactivated; RBAC already allows several holders, refuses to reach zero active holders, and warns at two-to-one.
nodes.source_location: Topic 4 — The super admin is an employee too

nodes.label: Version date rules (valid_until is inclusive)
nodes.rationale: valid_until is the last day the version was still correct. A printed field changing closes the old version yesterday and opens the new one today, or a document filed today would match the same person twice. Separation closes the open version today, which is what removes the person from later documents. A version begun today is corrected in place, and one closed earlier today is reopened, because a version covering only today cannot be what any document points at — the reopen rule was a bug found in testing.

nodes.label: Expo animation build sequence
nodes.rationale: Nine ordered steps for React Native: the same gate and purpose questions as the web skill, then thread choice, properties, spring or timing, keeping work off the JS thread, press instead of hover, haptics, and reduced motion. Feel is judged only on a release build on the slowest supported device.

nodes.label: Spring when a finger was involved
nodes.norm_label: spring when a finger was involved
nodes.rationale: Springs carry velocity through an interruption while timing curves restart, so any gesture uses a spring expressed as duration plus dampingRatio rather than mass/stiffness/damping. Bounce is earned only when the gesture carried momentum. Press feedback is 100-150ms, small state changes 150-200ms, sheets a ~300ms spring, and screen transitions keep the platform default.

nodes.label: Animation build sequence
nodes.rationale: Seven ordered steps — should it animate, what purpose, cheapest tool, which properties, easing or spring, interruption and exit, reduced motion and pointer gating. The order matters because steps 1 and 2 gate everything: reaching for a curve before knowing whether it animates at all is the failure the sequence exists to prevent.

nodes.label: Easing curves and duration budgets
nodes.rationale: ease-out for entering and exiting, ease-in-out for on-screen movement, linear for constant motion; never ease-in on UI because it delays the moment the user is watching. Built-in CSS easings are too weak, so cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1), (0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) and the iOS drawer curve (0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) are given exactly. UI animations stay under 300ms. Springs are for drag with momentum, interruptible gestures and elements that should feel alive.
nodes.source_location: 5. Easing and duration — or a spring

nodes.label: Eight audit categories
nodes.rationale: Purpose and frequency, easing and duration, physicality and origin, interruptibility, performance, accessibility, cohesion and tokens, and missed opportunities. The rule catalog with precise values lives here so audit subagents cite exact numbers rather than approximating.

nodes.label: Ten non-negotiable animation standards
nodes.rationale: Justified motion, frequency-appropriate motion, responsive easing, sub-300ms UI, origin and physical correctness, interruptibility, GPU-only properties, accessibility, asymmetric enter and exit, and cohesion. Default is to flag; approval is earned, because motion that merely runs but feels sluggish or lands from the wrong origin is a regression.

nodes.label: Expo animation recipes
nodes.rationale: Press feedback, drag-to-dismiss bottom sheet, swipe to delete, collapsing header, list entrances, keyboard-synced UI, tab indicator, Expo Router screen transitions, toast, and firing something once at a threshold, plus the shared setup and the two worklets every recipe needs.

nodes.label: Web animation recipes
nodes.rationale: Ready-to-build implementations for button press, dropdown and popover, tooltip, modal, drawer, toast, accordion, staggered group entrance, hold to confirm, tab indicator, scroll reveal, drag to dismiss, masking a crossfade, and programmatic animation without a library. Loaded when a request matches one, so the work starts from the recipe rather than a blank file.

nodes.label: Implementation plan template
nodes.rationale: Problem, target, repo conventions to follow, ordered steps, hard scope boundaries, and verification including a feel-check. Written for the weakest executor, stamped with the commit it was written against.

nodes.label: Animation standards reference
nodes.rationale: The precise-value catalog behind the review: frequency table, easing curves, per-element durations, physicality, springs, interruptibility, asymmetric timing, performance, transforms and clip-path, gestures and drag, masking imperfect crossfades, stagger, accessibility, debugging when feel is uncertain, and cohesion.

nodes.label: Haptics rules
nodes.rationale: Three absolute rules: fire in the same frame as the visual at the causal moment, one per user action, and never as the only feedback since haptics are off system-wide for many users and silent on most Android hardware. Used sparingly they make an app feel expensive; used everywhere they get turned off.

nodes.label: Press, not hover
nodes.rationale: Every hover affordance from the web has to be redesigned rather than ported. Feedback fires on press-in and commit on press-out, because waiting for the tap to complete feels dead. scale 0.97 over 100-150ms takes the label and icons with it, which is what reads as physical; touch targets stay 44x44pt with hitSlop rather than a grown visual.

nodes.label: Two runtimes — RN runtime and UI runtime
nodes.norm_label: two runtimes — rn runtime and ui runtime
nodes.rationale: Worklets make the split explicit: React renders on the RN runtime while worklets run every frame on the UI runtime. Motion that touches the RN runtime stutters as soon as the app does anything else, so the whole craft is keeping animation on the UI runtime. Mobile also has no hover, and the user's finger is on the element, which makes interruptibility and velocity handoff the baseline rather than polish.

nodes.label: Keep motion off the JS thread
nodes.norm_label: keep motion off the js thread
nodes.rationale: Never setState from a gesture or scroll handler — one React render per frame is the biggest cause of jank in RN apps. scheduleOnRN (which replaces the deprecated runOnJS) belongs in onEnd or a threshold reaction, never in onUpdate. Shared values are read and written with .get()/.set() in worklets and handlers only, never during render, and worklet-called functions need the 'worklet' directive or they throw on device while working in the debugger.
nodes.source_location: 6. Keep it off the JS thread

nodes.label: Frequency gate — should this animate at all
nodes.norm_label: frequency gate — should this animate at all
nodes.rationale: 100+ times a day gets no animation ever; tens a day gets near-imperceptible motion only; occasional gets standard; rare or first-time holds the delight budget. Keyboard-initiated actions are a disqualifier rather than a judgment call — Raycast has no open/close animation for exactly this reason. Producing zero lines of code is a success, not a dodge.

nodes.label: transform and opacity only
nodes.rationale: transform and opacity skip layout and paint and run on the GPU, while width, height, margin, padding, top and left trigger all three. clip-path is the sanctioned fourth and height is tolerated only for accordions. Never scale(0), since nothing in the real world appears from nothing; popovers scale from their trigger origin while modals stay centered; Motion's x/y/scale shorthands are not hardware accelerated.

nodes.label: Reduced motion and pointer gating ship with the animation
nodes.norm_label: reduced motion and pointer gating ship with the animation
nodes.rationale: Reduced motion means fewer and gentler, not zero: keep transitions that aid comprehension and drop movement. Hover motion is gated behind (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) because touch fires false hovers on tap.

nodes.label: Audit-then-plan workflow
nodes.rationale: Four phases — recon, parallel audit, vet and prioritize, write plans — so the capable model does the part where judgment compounds and execution goes to any agent, including cheaper models. Every finding is re-read at its file:line before being presented, and findings are ordered by leverage rather than by severity alone.

nodes.label: Read-only on source, self-contained plans
nodes.rationale: Only files under plans/ may be created or edited, and no installs, builds, commits or formatters run. Plans must inline exact paths, code excerpts, cubic-beziers and durations, because the executor has zero context from the conversation and zero taste of its own. Repository content is treated as inert data, and documented deliberate tradeoffs are not re-litigated.

nodes.label: Emil Kowalski's animation philosophy
nodes.rationale: The substantive craft bar (animations.dev) shared by the build, audit and review skills, so an animation written by one passes the review of another. The review method itself is adapted separately from aggressive code-quality review.

nodes.label: Debugging feel (slow motion, frame-by-frame, fresh eyes)
nodes.norm_label: debugging feel (slow motion, frame-by-frame, fresh eyes)

nodes.label: Never Ship table (web)
nodes.rationale: A self-check whose rows are each an automatic block in review-animations: transition: all, scale(0) entrances, ease-in on UI, animation on keyboard or high-frequency actions, over-300ms UI durations, centered transform-origin on anchored popovers, keyframes on rapidly-triggered elements, layout-property animation, ungated hover, missing reduced motion, everything entering at once.

nodes.label: Aggressive escalation triggers
nodes.rationale: Flagged on sight: transition: all, scale(0) entrances, ease-in on UI, animation on keyboard or 100+/day actions, over-300ms UI durations, centered origin on anchored popovers, keyframes on rapidly-triggered elements, layout-property animation, parent CSS variables driving child transforms, missing reduced motion, ungated hover, symmetric press timing, and everything entering at once.

nodes.label: Writing .drawio XML by hand
nodes.rationale: The geometry reference behind step 6 of the flowchart skill. Geometry hygiene matters more than it sounds, because a diagram whose arrows cross through boxes reads as careless and undermines trust in the content.

nodes.label: Flowchart diagrams skill
nodes.rationale: Exists because the default failure is not an ugly diagram but one that looks like a flowchart while having no grammar underneath — everything a rectangle, unlabelled branch arrows, explanations stuffed into nodes, and real decisions hidden in sticky notes. A flowchart is a small formal language whose whole point is that a reader can trace a path with a finger without reading every word.

nodes.label: Things that silently break
nodes.rationale: An mxGeometry without as="geometry" is ignored and the shape lands at 0,0; a source or target pointing at a missing id gives an edge floating in space with no error; two vertices sharing an id means draw.io drops one; overlapping notes just look broken. None of these raise an error, which is why the validator exists.

nodes.label: A worked critique of a failed diagram
nodes.norm_label: a worked critique of a failed diagram
nodes.rationale: A real diagram of what happens when an admin saves an edited employee record. It failed six ways: 76 percent one blue rectangle so shape carried no information, a process box with two unlabelled outgoing arrows where the missing question was the admin's answer, the two answers drawn as nodes instead of edge labels, two real branches (a permission gate and an absent Cancel path) hidden in sticky notes, an invisible client/server boundary that forced a box to say 'nothing is written yet' in prose, and a glossary sharing the canvas. The rebuild used three lanes, a parallelogram for the dialog, named exits including Cancel, cylinders per table, notes for explanations, and a separate glossary page.

nodes.label: Hunt the branches the prose forgot
nodes.norm_label: hunt the branches the prose forgot
nodes.rationale: Prose describes the happy path; exposing the gaps is most of a diagram's value. Walk the list explicitly: cancel or dismiss, permission gate, validation failure, empty or zero case, failure of the write itself, and already-in-that-state. Anything found that the source material did not mention goes to the user as a question, never into the diagram as an invention.

nodes.label: check_flowchart.py validator
nodes.rationale: Reports unlabelled decision exits, processes that branch without a decision, orphaned and dead-end nodes, prose crammed into nodes, overlapping geometry, broken edge references, and pages dominated by one shape type. It is a linter, not a judge: a deliberate second terminator is fine, a silently unlabelled branch is not. Then read one path end to end as a stranger would.

nodes.label: One cylinder = one table, one operation, one point in the flow
nodes.norm_label: one cylinder = one table, one operation, one point in the flow
nodes.rationale: 'writes' is not an operation — the reader cannot tell an insert from an update, which is usually the whole point of the step, and reads escape this only because a read has one meaning. The shape is a noun (the table name) and the arrow is a verb (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/UPSERT), kept bare because row counts crowd the busiest part of the canvas and go stale. Never two tables in one cylinder, never a read and a write on one, and the same table touched twice is two cylinders — collapsing them hides the gap where the interesting behaviour lives.

nodes.label: Every decision exit carries a label
nodes.norm_label: every decision exit carries a label
nodes.rationale: An unlabelled branch forces the reader to infer the condition from the destination box, which defeats the diamond. Exits must be mutually exclusive and cover every case, and the diamond holds the question while the answer sits on the arrow.

nodes.label: Check it is actually a flowchart
nodes.norm_label: check it is actually a flowchart
nodes.rationale: Forcing the wrong content into a flowchart is a bigger failure than bad shapes. Comparisons want a table, before/after wants two panels, 'what talks to what' wants an architecture diagram with no start node, and a glossary belongs on its own page — sitting beside a flow it steals attention and is the commonest way a good flow gets buried.

nodes.label: Mermaid as the alternative output
nodes.rationale: Better when the diagram belongs in a README, a code comment or a chat reply — the same grammar with less ceremony, and only the geometry work disappears. Reach for drawio when the user needs to edit it by hand or the diagram is large enough that manual layout beats auto-layout.

nodes.label: Write the node list before touching XML
nodes.norm_label: write the node list before touching xml
nodes.rationale: One line per node tagged with shape and actor, because this catches structural problems while they are still cheap to fix. Two tests fall out of it: any node whose text needs the word 'and' is two nodes, and any node with more than one outgoing arrow is a missing decision.

nodes.label: Shape grammar (six shapes, no more)
nodes.rationale: Stadium for start and end, rectangle for a system step, diamond for a question, parallelogram for what a person sees or answers, cylinder for a table, sticky note for why rather than what. Consistency is what makes shapes readable; a seventh shape invented for one node teaches the reader nothing. Node text works best at twelve words or fewer, asides belong in notes on dashed connectors, and a legend near the title makes the grammar self-teaching.

nodes.label: Tab indicator via duplicated clipped copy
nodes.norm_label: tab indicator via duplicated clipped copy

nodes.label: Absolutely positioned childless element width exception
nodes.norm_label: absolutely positioned childless element width exception

nodes.label: transform and opacity are free; everything else is a layout pass
nodes.norm_label: transform and opacity are free; everything else is a layout pass

nodes.label: Asymmetric timing where the user is deciding
nodes.norm_label: asymmetric timing where the user is deciding

nodes.label: Commit Primary Changes Scope
nodes.rationale: Stages only the files created or modified while completing the current session's task, named one by one instead of git add -A. When the session holds no completed task the files may have changed for reasons never observed, so the correct move is to ask which files are primary rather than guess.

nodes.label: Commit Staged Files Scope
nodes.rationale: Commits exactly the existing index, read with git diff --cached --name-only, and stages nothing new. When the index is empty the run stops and says so rather than guessing at something to add.

nodes.label: Commit This Scope
nodes.rationale: The default when no scope is named: git add -A sweeps modified, deleted, and untracked files. Whatever got swept in that is not the main work is called out in the trailing bullet, and a file that should not be in the repo at all is named and left out rather than committed quietly.

nodes.label: Pre-Commit Format Check
nodes.rationale: A closing checklist re-verifies the staging scope, the prefix and lowercase title, the blank line after it, main-before-unrelated ordering, a bullet or two-space wrap on every body line, the 72-character limit, and the absence of trailers.

nodes.label: No Commit Trailers
nodes.rationale: No Co-Authored-By trailer and no generated-with footer are permitted anywhere in the message.

nodes.label: Bullet Body
nodes.rationale: The body is bullets only, wrapped at 72 characters with two-space continuation indents, one bullet per logical change, three to six bullets in total. Identifiers are written out literally. A commit that needs more than six bullets is probably doing too much and should be split.

nodes.label: Commit Message Format
nodes.rationale: The repo enforces one house shape for commit messages so history stays scannable: a conventional prefix and short lowercase title, a blank line, then a wrapped bullet list. Prose paragraphs are rejected because they bury several logical changes in one block.

nodes.label: Conventional Prefix Title
nodes.rationale: The title takes a conventional prefix (feat, fix, refactor, chore, docs, test), a lowercase first letter, no trailing period, and stays under about 72 characters. Previously untracked files are feat rather than refactor, because nothing existed yet to refactor.

nodes.label: Default Body Ordering
nodes.rationale: Main changes come first, most important first, then anything swept into the same commit that is not part of that work. Trailing bullets stay short; an unrelated change big enough to need its own explanation belongs in its own commit instead.

nodes.label: Staging Scope
nodes.rationale: Which files get staged is settled before the message is written, because the wrong scope forces an amend or a reset afterwards. Three phrases select the scope and the widest one is also the default; the scope is never widened on the agent's own initiative.

nodes.label: Firing once at a threshold with useAnimatedReaction
nodes.norm_label: firing once at a threshold with useanimatedreaction

nodes.label: Haptics rules (same frame, one per action, never the only feedback)
nodes.norm_label: haptics rules (same frame, one per action, never the only feedback)

nodes.norm_label: 'worklet' directive on functions called from a worklet

nodes.norm_label: two runtimes (rn runtime vs ui runtime)

nodes.norm_label: phase 2 — parallel audit with read-only subagents

nodes.norm_label: denr official seal (department of environment and natural resources, 1987)

nodes.norm_label: government agency identity of the ems deployment

nodes.norm_label: seal iconography: stylized tree, blue sky, green terraced land

nodes.label: Philippine Flag Motif (Eight-Rayed Sun and Three Stars)
nodes.norm_label: philippine flag motif (eight-rayed sun and three stars)

nodes.label: git feature flow
nodes.rationale: The whole workflow exists to control the shape of the graph on main - a short list of merge bubbles, one per feature, plus a few app-level commits, so `git log --graph` on main shows what landed and when without every intermediate commit.

nodes.label: deciding where a change belongs
nodes.rationale: Feature work goes on its feature branch; config, dependencies, tooling, docs and cross-cutting fixes go directly on main; a change touching several features goes as one honest mixed commit on main, because splitting it would create three half-merges and a tangled graph. When the bucket is unclear, ask rather than guess - guessing wrong means rewriting history.

nodes.label: stop and report on merge conflicts
nodes.norm_label: stop and report on merge conflicts
nodes.rationale: A conflict during main into feature usually means a real overlap the user needs to see, so never resolve by picking a side automatically and never abort silently.

nodes.label: leave merged feature branches alive
nodes.rationale: Branches here are long-lived - the user returns to a feature weeks later, merges main into it again and keeps going. Deleting merged branches is a common git reflex and is wrong in this repo.

nodes.label: merge asymmetry
nodes.rationale: feature into main is always --no-ff because the merge commit IS the record of the feature; main into feature is a plain merge where fast-forward is preferred, because bubbles inside a feature branch add noise. Rebase and squash are forbidden between these branches unless explicitly asked - both destroy the topology the workflow exists to preserve.

nodes.label: never push
nodes.rationale: Pushing is the user's last checkpoint before anything leaves the machine. Local commits and merges are fine; git fetch and other read-only remote commands are the one exception.

nodes.label: The finger is on the element (gesture-first input)
nodes.norm_label: the finger is on the element (gesture-first input)

nodes.label: Default to flagging; approval is earned
nodes.norm_label: default to flagging; approval is earned

nodes.label: admin:view_employees and admin:manage_employees
nodes.rationale: A new `employees` submodule in PERMISSION_DEFS so a clerk can keep the staff list current without also being able to create accounts and assign roles. The Users page still lists employees without needing view_employees, since the key guards the page rather than reading names elsewhere.

nodes.label: No separate admin:correct_employees key, for now
nodes.norm_label: no separate admin:correct_employees key, for now
nodes.rationale: Adding the key would take away an ability roles already have on day one, against a small risk in an office with two logins where every repair is already attributed. Adding it later is one PERMISSION_DEFS entry and two guards, while removing a key roles depend on is the harder direction. Decided by Claude, not the user, and recorded so it can be overruled.

nodes.label: sync-permissions backfills the super-admin role
nodes.rationale: The super-admin role is frozen in the role editor, so a new admin:* key it does not already hold could never be granted through the interface. Re-normalizing does not help because implication only runs upward. The script now finds that role by the permission admin:manage_roles rather than by name, inserts missing admin:* keys in one transaction, names what it added, and skips cleanly on a fresh database.
nodes.source_location: Topic 6 — The missing step was added

nodes.label: Two admin pages: Employees and Users
nodes.norm_label: two admin pages: employees and users
nodes.rationale: One dialog for both records would ask for fourteen things; the two lists are different sizes so a merged page would carry empty account columns; and keeping the staff list current is clerical work while creating a login decides who may do what. Accepted cost: hiring somebody who needs a login means visiting two pages.

nodes.label: Primary and Foreign Key Naming
nodes.rationale: Semantic foreign key names are allowed where the name does not match the referenced table, documented inline in the schema file.

nodes.label: Snake Case Columns, Camel Case Fields
nodes.norm_label: snake case columns, camel case fields
nodes.rationale: Mapped in the Drizzle schema so the database and TypeScript each keep their own convention.

nodes.label: Soft Delete via Status Enum
nodes.rationale: A status enum rather than a boolean flag, so more than two lifecycle states stay expressible.

nodes.label: Keep every edge parented to the root
nodes.norm_label: keep every edge parented to the root
nodes.rationale: An edge parented to a lane is clipped by that lane, even when its endpoints live in different lanes. Use orthogonalEdgeStyle for right-angle routing, put the branch condition in the edge's value, and draw annotation connectors dashed with no arrowhead so they read as commentary rather than as a step.

nodes.label: Child geometry is relative to the lane
nodes.norm_label: child geometry is relative to the lane
nodes.rationale: The single most common source of 'why is my node outside the lane': child x/y are measured from the lane's top-left corner and the title bar is inside that box, so with startSize=40 a child at y=70 sits 30px below it. Set collapsible=0 so a reader cannot accidentally fold a lane shut, and avoid childLayout=stackLayout on the pool, which re-flows children and fights the coordinates you chose.

nodes.label: Swimlanes for actor boundaries
nodes.rationale: Use them when steps cross a boundary the reader needs to see, such as browser/server/database, because lanes make visible a fact prose inside boxes cannot show — for example that a flow crosses to the server twice, once to read and once to write. Skip them when everything happens in one place, where they only cost width.

nodes.label: WAAPI programmatic animation without a library
nodes.norm_label: waapi programmatic animation without a library

nodes.label: Cheapest tool that works (web tool ladder)
nodes.norm_label: cheapest tool that works (web tool ladder)

nodes.label: EMS — Environmental Management System (project brief)
nodes.rationale: Built for DENR-PENRO Dinagat Islands to track fuel, electricity, water and paper consumption plus ESWM and GHG compliance. Around five to ten concurrent users and fewer than twenty in total, one office, no multi-branch support.

nodes.label: Fully offline LAN deployment
nodes.rationale: No internet dependency, accessible only inside the office network. Implies adapter-node rather than adapter-auto, no CDN-hosted assets, fonts or scripts, and session-based auth with no OAuth. Roughly 60 percent of clients are on WiFi, so session handling, form submissions and loading states must fail gracefully and recover rather than assume a rock-solid link.

nodes.label: ISO 14001:2015 compliance
nodes.rationale: The environmental management standard the tracked data supports compliance with. It is the reason the six consumption and compliance areas are the scope.

nodes.label: The six tracked areas
nodes.rationale: Fuel, electricity, water, paper, ESWM and GHG. Each becomes both a staff module and an admin submodule in the permission definitions, and each will eventually need its own report documents.

nodes.label: Reserve a routing channel
nodes.rationale: drawio routes an unconstrained orthogonal edge through whatever is in the way, so a merge arrow will happily cut through the other branch's box. Leave an empty column inside the lane and pin the merge edge to it with exitX/entryX, or stagger the y values. Crossings between a control arrow and a data arrow are acceptable and normal; an arrow crossing through a box is not.

nodes.label: A vertical grid for row positions
nodes.norm_label: a vertical grid for row positions
nodes.rationale: Pick row positions in advance with 60-90px of clear space so labels have room. Diamonds need to be wide — 400x150 for a one-line question — because a cramped diamond wraps its text into an unreadable sliver.

nodes.label: Add name or position change dialog
nodes.norm_label: add name or position change dialog
nodes.rationale: src/routes/admin/employees/add-change-dialog.svelte. Ends the current history row and starts a new one — the 'record a change that happened' path.

nodes.label: Correct this entry dialog
nodes.rationale: src/routes/admin/employees/correct-entry-dialog.svelte, opened from name-position-history-sheet.svelte. Edits a row in place — the 'fix a mistake in what was typed' path — and carries the warning headed 'This corrects what is already filed'. Two separate entry points replaced the originally planned single Save button that asked which kind of change it was.

nodes.label: Org unit guard (src/lib/server/org-unit-guard.ts)
nodes.rationale: One function answering whether an org unit is named by a setting, called by both the delete and deactivate paths in src/routes/admin/org-structure/+page.server.ts. A real foreign key would only have protected deletion; deactivation is an ordinary column change no foreign key can catch, so one mechanism covering both beats two covering one each. The cost, accepted knowingly, is that it holds only while every path goes through it.

nodes.label: src/lib/rbac/access.ts helpers
nodes.rationale: Every access check tests a permission key, never a role name, because role names are runtime data an admin can rename while keys are defined in source and cannot change underneath the code.

nodes.label: create-admin.ts bootstrap
nodes.rationale: Runs on the production server after build via tsx, reading source rather than build output. Finds the super-admin role by permission, never by name, because a role name is runtime data an admin can rename.

nodes.label: expandPermissions
nodes.rationale: Walks the implication chain all the way up and is idempotent, so it is safe to apply anywhere. Unrecognised keys pass through untouched rather than being dropped, so a leftover database row never silently removes access it was already granting.

nodes.label: hooks.server.ts route guard
nodes.rationale: The normal permission guard already blocks an admin user typing a staff URL, so nothing special is needed to keep the two kinds of role apart at the route level.

nodes.label: PERMISSION_DEFS
nodes.rationale: The single source in src/lib/server/permissions.ts. Permissions are developer-defined at build time and an admin never creates or edits one, so a new module or action is added there and nowhere else.

nodes.label: PERMISSION_IMPLIES
nodes.rationale: Stores single steps only and must never be read directly.

nodes.label: PERMISSIONS
nodes.rationale: Records submodule at build time while the parts were still separate, which is why a key's submodule is looked up rather than computed. UI grouping reads this in TypeScript, not the permission table row and not the key string.

nodes.label: Role templates
nodes.rationale: Pre-checked defaults only, never saved as records of their own. The Admin template is derived by filtering the Roles keys out rather than listing keys by hand, so a new admin page is picked up automatically while the Roles page stays excluded.

nodes.label: sync-permissions.ts
nodes.rationale: Permission rows are data, not schema, so drizzle-kit generate produces nothing for a new key and this script must be run after any PERMISSION_DEFS change. Orphan deletion is always offered and never skipped, because 'missing from the code' could mean removed for good or absent from the checked-out branch and the script cannot tell them apart, while which roles held a key is recorded nowhere but the database. Grants are deleted before permission rows because role_permission.permission_fk has no onDelete and MySQL restricts.

nodes.label: Config table
nodes.rationale: One row per setting, key fixed in code and plain-text value filled in by the office, so no row id is hardcoded. Typed columns were rejected because only one row would ever use them; a short fixed code column on org_unit was rejected because an admin-populated but non-editable field confuses whoever maintains office data. Lives at src/lib/server/db/schema/config.ts with CONFIG_KEYS beside it so a typo is a type error.

nodes.label: Where a default name comes from
nodes.norm_label: where a default name comes from
nodes.rationale: Partly settled. Three sources: set by an admin (the fuel approver), worked out by the report (RIS 'Requested by' defaults to whoever is entering), or set by whoever handles the report (raised, not yet needed). The rule is not 'defaults are never configured' but 'configured here only when nothing else can work it out'.

nodes.label: employee_history table
nodes.rationale: Holds one dated version of a person's name, position title and short form so an old document keeps the wording it was printed with. Built 31 August 2026; the current columns stay on employee as a copy written in the same transaction, because reading a name is the common case and reaching through history rows everywhere would be a lot of code for no gain.

nodes.label: employee_history_correction log
nodes.rationale: A spelling fix edits a version in place and corrects every document at once, which would otherwise leave no trace; the log records field, old value, new value and who did it so the repair stays accountable.

nodes.label: Employee and user separation
nodes.rationale: Option 1, full separation, was chosen over leaving employees only for non-users (people would live in two tables) and over letting user be the employee table (login code would have to exclude password-less rows forever, easy to get wrong). Built; details in .claude/docs/features/employee-and-user-separation.md.

nodes.label: Fuel report
nodes.rationale: Not one form but three documents printed together, which corrected Topic 5's assumption that a report equals a form; the decision survived and now applies per document.

nodes.label: fuel.usual_approver setting
nodes.rationale: An optional default employee id, added 8 September 2026 after fuel.penr_officer was removed. It only decides which name the form starts with; nothing is restricted and nothing is fixed. A stored id belonging to somebody separated simply reads as empty rather than warning anyone.

nodes.label: Group designation title
nodes.rationale: A title on a Technical Working Group, association or BAC Secretariat is printed on the paper, so it is a caption and needs no mechanism. Group titles appear on that group's own memoranda rather than on the fill-in forms this project handles, and are never reused across documents. This settlement also retired the coined terms 'position signatory' and 'designation signatory'.

nodes.label: General Services Unit (GSU)
nodes.rationale: There is only one General Services Unit and any of its staff may approve any section's slip; an earlier sketch giving the roster its own org unit so GSU and CDS copies expected different people was wrong and was dropped.

nodes.label: OIC (Officer-in-Charge)
nodes.rationale: Two senses at this office: the standing OIC who has held the post for years and whose name is printed, and temporary cover for a few days that is only ever handwritten. Neither needs anything built.

nodes.label: org.gsu_unit setting
nodes.rationale: Names the org unit whose staff may be offered on a GSU-restricted block. Renamed from fuel.gsu_org_unit on 7 September 2026 because which unit is the General Services Unit is a fact about the office, not about fuel, and two documents read it — a per-report copy could disagree with itself.

nodes.label: Per procurationem (p.p.) signing
nodes.rationale: Signing on somebody else's behalf with their authority, confirmed on four blocks of the real CDS copies. Entirely invisible to the system: the printed name never changes and everything the substitute adds is handwritten.

nodes.label: Position title short form
nodes.rationale: Documents print 'AO-I/Supply Officer', not 'Administrative Officer I (Supply Officer)'; the boxes on the paper are small. No rule worth trusting derives one from the other, so somebody types it once. One person has exactly one short form, so it lives on the employee rather than per document.

nodes.label: Somebody no longer working is never offered and never saves
nodes.norm_label: somebody no longer working is never offered and never saves
nodes.rationale: Any employment_status other than active counts as not working. No warning is raised when somebody is marked separated: the next person to prepare a slip finds them gone and picks whoever signs now, which is how the office already works.

nodes.label: Signatories page (/admin/signatories)
nodes.rationale: A tab per report, and inside a tab one row per setting rather than one row per document: four rows would be four controls over two stored values, promising an independence that does not exist. Placed next to Organizational Structure but kept separate because this is signatory configuration, not office structure.

nodes.label: Signature block
nodes.rationale: Settled as the single word for the whole printed block (label, name, printed title) after 'signing line' had been used loosely for both the block and its label.

nodes.label: Supplier signature block
nodes.rationale: The gasoline station owner or their staff is not an employee and not in the system. Handled by the block's rule being 'nobody may be chosen' and printing blank, rather than by inventing a record for them.

nodes.label: Rule: where the printed title comes from
nodes.norm_label: rule: where the printed title comes from
nodes.rationale: Two answers only: nothing is printed because the form carries a caption, or the person's own position title as it stood at the time. There is no third rule for a fixed string written into the program.

nodes.label: Rule: who may be chosen for a block
nodes.norm_label: rule: who may be chosen for a block
nodes.rationale: Any employee, only staff of a named unit, or nobody at all. Only a restricted list needs a rule and only the GSU one is restricted. Choosing the wrong eligible person is not the system's problem — GSU simply refuses to sign; the system only stops what is impossible.

nodes.label: Admin role
nodes.rationale: Holds only admin:* keys and works inside /admin/*. A staff permission is unusable to an admin user because their navigation shows only admin pages and the hooks.server.ts guard blocks a typed staff URL, so the two kinds are never mixed in one role.

nodes.label: Fuel approve permission key (still open)
nodes.rationale: Fuel is the only module with an approval step, so it is the only one needing an approve key: a staff member requests a withdrawal slip, GSU approves it physically with a signature, and the key controls who may afterwards mark it approved. Electricity, water, paper, ESWM and GHG record data without approval. Exact key list undecided.

nodes.label: Role editor
nodes.rationale: Asks which kind of role up front and then shows only that key set. Saves exactly what was ticked, since auto-tick already includes every implied key, but still runs expandPermissions server-side because a POST can be crafted in the browser.

nodes.label: Staff role
nodes.rationale: Holds only non-admin keys and works inside the staff routes. Admin data pages mirror the staff ones as separate routes rather than one route branching on permissions, because the admin table has features the staff table does not.

nodes.label: Super-admin role
nodes.rationale: Identified by a live condition — does the role hold admin:manage_roles, read from role_permission — rather than an is_protected column. Frozen: only description is editable; name, status and permission set are locked; deletion, deactivation and duplication are blocked. Exactly one holder role, never zero active users, and it can only be granted by someone who already holds it or by the bootstrap script.

nodes.label: Commit prefix convention
nodes.rationale: Conventional prefix with a lowercase first letter; untracked or new files are feat: rather than refactor:.

nodes.label: EMS technology stack
nodes.rationale: SvelteKit with Svelte 5 runes, TypeScript, Tailwind, shadcn-svelte, Drizzle ORM on MySQL 8.4, adapter-node. Fully offline on a LAN server, so no CDN assets, no external auth providers and no runtime network calls.

nodes.label: Requisition and Issue Slip (RIS)
nodes.rationale: The only fuel document printing real position titles, which is why it drives the employee history requirement; its 'Approved by' was wrongly recorded as a fixed string 'OIC, PENR Officer' and is in fact a picked person whose own title prints.

nodes.label: Signature blocks are fixed in the code
nodes.norm_label: signature blocks are fixed in the code
nodes.rationale: Blocks sit in fixed positions on the printed page. An admin-editable list would let the layout be broken, so the set of blocks is program and database structure, one column per block holding an employee history reference or nothing. The known cost is that adding or renaming a block is developer work.

nodes.label: Caption
nodes.rationale: A title printed on the paper itself ('Driver', 'Section Incharge', 'GSU Representative'). The test is where the words come from, not what they look like: a caption is identical under any name, so the system stores nothing for it. This realisation removed roughly half the storage problem and killed the separate signatory table.

nodes.label: Documents store a reference, never typed text
nodes.norm_label: documents store a reference, never typed text
nodes.rationale: Storing the name as text freezes both a real name change and a typo the same way. If 30 records were saved with a misspelled name nobody would remember which 30. A link to a history row lets a correction reach every record and a marriage leave old records alone.

nodes.label: The selection list is built from the document's filed date
nodes.norm_label: the selection list is built from the document's filed date
nodes.rationale: The form asks who was valid on the filed date, comparing valid_from and valid_until, rather than who is working today. Reopening last month's slip still offers last month's people, a slip filed today does not, and editing needs no special case. Separation must therefore close the current history row, not only change the status.

nodes.label: The separate signatory table was removed
nodes.norm_label: the separate signatory table was removed
nodes.rationale: The whole design had rested on the assumption that a signatory is a person with a typed name and typed position title in a table of their own. Real fuel documents examined 27 August 2026 showed nobody's title is ever typed: it is a caption, or fixed, or read from the person's record. Cost an edit and nothing more, because nothing had been built. A per-report signatory table was also rejected: anybody signing two kinds of document would need a row in each, so a spelling fix would have to be repeated.

nodes.label: Signing happens on paper only
nodes.rationale: The system prepares and prints the correct names; the paper is carried around and signed by hand. An earlier answer saying signing happened both on paper and in the system created a problem that no longer exists — signers without an account could never approve, so 'not signed yet' and 'never signed here' were indistinguishable.

nodes.label: One person may fill two blocks of the same document
nodes.norm_label: one person may fill two blocks of the same document
nodes.rationale: Allowed with no warning. The user watched an office head approve their own leave application when the admin officer was away; that observed case outweighed the written rule. It is the document, not the person, that decides whether one name may fill two blocks.

nodes.label: Role editor auto-tick rule
nodes.rationale: Ticking any non-view action ticks that module's view, because managing a page you cannot open is meaningless; unticking view clears every other action in the module. This is what makes the stored ticked set already closed under implication.

nodes.label: No user changes their own role
nodes.norm_label: no user changes their own role
nodes.rationale: Prevents self-promotion and also self-lockout, where an admin strips their own admin:manage_users and loses the only page that could undo it. Together with 'only a super-admin assigns super-admin' it closes the grant path completely in both directions.

nodes.label: Permission key shape
nodes.rationale: Keys are built forward and never split back apart: '_' is both the separator and a legal character inside a submodule name, so admin:view_org_units reads equally well as view + org_units or view_org + units and nothing in the string resolves it. One level of submodules only, every module must define view because that is the key each route's load checks, plural for countable things, and data modules appear twice on purpose.

nodes.label: Roles page restriction
nodes.rationale: Both Roles keys are absent from the role editor rather than greyed out, so no admin can violate the one-holder rule through the UI and the holder check exists only as a safety net. admin:view_roles is withheld alongside admin:manage_roles because a Roles page nobody can edit has no reason to exist, so its read-only rendering is never built — the one admin page that does not follow the view/manage split.

nodes.label: drizzle-kit push rule
nodes.rationale: Schema changes reach the database only through drizzle-kit push, and it is never run unannounced — the user is asked whether to run it themselves or to have it run for them.

nodes.label: Graphify only when asked by name
nodes.norm_label: graphify only when asked by name
nodes.rationale: A question about this codebase is an ordinary question answered by reading files, even though graphify-out/ exists in the repo and the graphify skill invites its use.

nodes.label: Read schema/index.ts fresh before any query or table change
nodes.norm_label: read schema/index.ts fresh before any query or table change
nodes.rationale: src/lib/server/db/schema/index.ts must be read fresh rather than worked from a remembered copy.
